title: Luke 23
description: Luke 23 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
topics: forgive them for they know not what they do
today you will be with me in paradise
into your hands I commit my spirit
paragraphs: 1 Then the whole assembly of them got up and led him away to Pilate. 2 They began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man subverting our people, forbidding people to pay the tribute to Caesar, and claiming that he is Christ,a a king.”
3 So Pilate asked Jesus,b “Are you the king of the Judeans?”c
But in answer, Jesusd said to him, “You yourself are saying it.”e
4 Pilate said to the lead priests and the crowds, “I don’t find any basis for charges against this person.”
5 But they escalated, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, having started in Galilee and come all the way here!”

6 At hearing that, Pilate demanded to know whether the person was Galilean, 7 and after learning that he was from Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who himself was also in Jerusalem during those days. 8 At seeing Jesus, Herod was overjoyed because he had been wanting to see him for a considerable time, since he had heard about him and was hoping to see some sign brought about by him. 9 So Herodf questioned him for a considerable time, but Jesusg did not answer him at all. 10 The lead priests and scripture scholars stood there, forcefully making accusations against him. 11 Herod, together with his soldiers, after treating him as worthless and mocking him, dressing him in radiant clothing, sent him back to Pilate. 12 Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that day, whereas there had been hostility between them.

13 Pilate called together the lead priests, the leaders, and the people. 14 He told them, “You brought me this person as inciting the people,h but as you see, when I examined him right in front of you, I did not find in connection with this person any basis for the charges with which you accused him. 15 Neither did Herod, since he sent back to us. Look, he has done nothing worthy of death. 16 Therefore, after I have him whipped, I will release him.”

18 i They all burst out shouting together, “Take this one away! Release Barabbasj for us!” 19 (This was someone who had been thrown in prison for an insurrection that had started in the city and murder.)
20 Pilate addressed them again, wanting to release Jesus.
21 But they kept shouting, “Crucify! Crucify him!”

22 For the third time, he said to them, “Why? What harm did this man do? I have found no cause for a sentence of death in connection with him. Therefore, after I have him whipped, I will release him.”
23 But they pressed him with loud shouts, demanding that he be crucified, and their shouts were overpowering.
24 So, Pilate ruled that their demand should happen. 25 He released the one they demanded, who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, but handed Jesus over for what they desired.

26 As they led him away, they seized Simeonk of Cyrene, who was coming from the countryside, and set the cross upon him to carry it behind Jesus. 27 A huge crowd of the people followed him, including women who were beating their chestsl and wailing for him.

28 Turning to them, Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, don’t weep for me, but weep for yourselves and your children 29 because—look—the days are coming when theym will say, ‘How greatly fortunaten are women who cannot have children,o wombs that did not give birth, and breasts that did not nurse!’p 30 Then ‘they will say to the mountains, “Fall on us!” and to the hills, “Bury us!”’q 31 because if things like these are done while the wood is wet, what will happen when it is dry?”

32 Two other criminalsr were also led to be executeds along with him. 33 When they came to the place called “The Skull,” they crucified him and the criminals there, with one to the right and the other to the left.
34 Jesus said, “Father, let go of thist for them, since they don’t know what they’re doing.”u Then they divided his clothing by throwing lots.v
35 The people stood there watching, but the leaders began scoffing at him, saying, “He liberatedw others; let him liberate himself if he is the Christx of God, the chosen one!”

36 The soldiers also mocked him, approaching and offering him sour winey 37 and saying, “If you are the king of the Judeans,z liberate yourself!” 38 There was also an inscription over him: “This is the king of the Judeans.”
39 One of the criminals who was hanging there spoke to him contemptuously, “Aren’t you the Christ? Liberate yourself and us!”

40 In response, the other one reprimanded him, saying, “Don’t you take God seriously, since you are undergoing the same sentence! 41 While it is right for us, since we are getting what is appropriate for what we did, this person did nothing wrong.” 42 Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your reign.”
43 Jesus told him, “Honestly, I’m telling you, today you will be with me in the Garden.”aa
44 When it reached about noon,bb darkness came over the whole land until midafternooncc 45 when the sun’s light failed. The temple curtaindd was split down the middle.
46 Calling out with a loud voice, Jesus said, “Father, into your hands I entrust my life-breath.”ee After saying this, he breathed out.

47 At seeing what happened, the centurionff praised God, saying, “This person truly was innocent!”gg 48 And all the crowds that had come together to see the spectacle, after watching what happened, returned beating their chests.hh 49 All those who knew him were standing at a distance, and the women who had followed him together from Galilee saw these things.

50 Significantly,ii there was a man named Joseph who was a member of the council,jj and he was a generouskk and justll man 51 (He was not one who had agreed with their intention and action). He was from Arimathea, a Judean town, and he was anticipating God’s Reign. 52 Having approached Pilate, he requested Jesus’ body. 53 After taking it down, he wrapped it with linen cloth and placed it in a tomb cut into the rockmm where no one had yet been laid. 54 It was the day of preparationnn and Shabbat was beginning.oo 55 The women who had accompanied Jesus from Galilee, followed and saw the tomb as his body was placed inside. 56 After returning, they prepared aromatic spices and perfumed oils, and while it was Shabbat, they restedpp according to the direction.qq

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: The word Ioudaioi can mean either ‘Judeans’ or ‘Jews.’ The context of this incident is in Jerusalem, a prominent city of the Roman province of Judea, over which Pilate was governor.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: The Greek reads su legeis, which literally means “you say [it]” or “you speak [it].” This is the same wording as in Matthew 27:11 and Mark 15:2 and similar wording as Luke 22:70 (“You yourselves are saying that I am”). The phrase indirectly reflects the speaker’s words without direct affirmation or denial. Jesus’ choice of this response subtly shifts responsibility back to the questioner, often signaling both acknowledgment and reservation. Rather than confirming, Jesus lets their words “stand” on their own.

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: The name ‘Herod’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘turning the people away’, implying turning them against the authorities.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Verse 17, which reads, “(Now he was obligated to release one individual for them at the feast.),” is absent from the oldest and seemingly most reliable manuscripts. Scholars suggest it was original to Matthew 27:15 and Mark 15:6 and it was later added to Luke.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: ‘Barabbas’ was Aramaic for ‘Son of Father’, which could have been his father’s name (Abba) or it could have been a title or pseudonym of some kind.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Simon.’ Simon is the English transliteration of the Greek transliteration of Simeon. There’s a long history of de-Jewish-ing the names of people in the Bible, including Jesus (Joshua) that stems from pervasive antisemitism.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: Beating one’s chest was a cultural display of mourning.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: This is referring to the children of the women Jesus is addressing.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘blessed.’ There is no single English word that covers what is being described here. This word is makarios, and its Hebrew counterpart is ashrei. It is unrelated to eulogeo (both in what it means and in the linguistic root it comes from) and to eulogeo’s Hebrew counterpart baruch, the other word traditionally translated ‘blessed’ (Matthew 21:9; 23:39). Eulogeo is to praise someone or to ‘speak well’ over someone, declaring goodwill for that person, as a benediction. Makarios is not praise, well-wishes, or benediction. It is a declaration, a communal act of calling attention to someone having everything one could need or desire, and being positioned such that everyone would acknowledge without doubt that the person was the peak version of fortunate or well-off, a sense of absolute well-being. It was used of people with power, with victory over enemies, with wealth, and it was even what Greeks called their gods, who were beyond lack and beyond the reach of circumstances, which is why declaring it of people who are poor or grieving would have been completely surprising and even baffling.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: Or ‘infertile women’

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: Essentially, these cries indicate they will wish they had never been born.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: Citation of Hosea 10:8

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: The phrasing ‘other criminals’ implies that Jesus was a criminal as well, which by the strict definition of someone who was tried and sentenced for a crime, he was. It then becomes important to note that ‘criminal’ is not necessarily a synonym for guilty party, only someone who was designated as guilty by people with power. There’s a thematic connection with Jesus’ reference to Isaiah 53:12 in Luke 22:37, though the word for ‘criminal’ here is not the same one used in chapter 22 or in Isaiah.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: Or ‘lifted up’ or ‘done away with’

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: The word here, traditionally translated as “forgive,” is never directed toward a person but always directed toward what the person owes. For example, it would not be accurate to phrase it as “forgive us for our debts” but rather “forgive our debts for us.” It’s about sending away, distancing, releasing, letting go, separating from oneself, abandoning or disconnecting from something.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: This sentence is included in many early and reliable manuscripts and omitted from others that are also early and reliable. Some reasons for thinking it may be original is that it is not in Matthew or Mark, and there is a parallel statement in Acts 7:60, which is also written by Luke; however, some use that to suggest that it was added to Luke based on being in Acts. The SBLGNT includes it here, and the LIT is following that decision.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: Reference to Psalm 22 (especially verse 18). Literally, it means ‘throwing lots.’ ‘Lots’ were any objects marked with names or other symbols to identify whose was chosen when they shook the collection and noted the first one to fall.

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘saved.’ This word carries a meaning of any kind of action to prevent or repair harm. Appropriate translations could be ‘liberated,’ ‘restored,’ ‘rescued,’ ‘healed,’ ‘preserved,’ or ‘protected.’

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: Roman soldiers often drank wine that had gone to vinegar mixed with water. It also seems to be a reference to Psalm 69:21.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: The word Ioudaioi can mean either ‘Judeans’ or ‘Jews.’ The context of this incident is in Jerusalem, a prominent city in the Roman province of Judea, over which Pilate was governor.

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Paradise.’ The word paradeisos came from the Persian word for a walled garden or royal park. The Septuagint used it for the garden in Eden, and Jewish writings of Jesus’ time used it for Eden restored in the coming Age as well as for where those aligned with God’s path are present with God. It was not a synonym for the later idea of Heaven as a destination. The exchange suggests a reversal: the man asks to be remembered when Jesus comes into his reign (v. 42), and Jesus answers with the language of a king’s garden, opened to someone the empire executed and the implied promise that he will be present with the anointed king during his reign.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: Reference to Amos 8:1–14 (especially verse 9)

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘sixth hour’ and ‘ninth hour’

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: See Leviticus 16:2, 15–17 and Leviticus 21:16–23. There are also other places the curtain is mentioned. With these two places in mind, see Isaiah 56:1–8 with the other references Jesus has made to Isaiah 56 building a strong connection between what Jesus is about, Leviticus 16 and 21, and Isaiah 56.

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: Quotation of Psalm 31:5

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: Centurions were a type of Roman military officer.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: Or ‘just’ or ‘right’ or ‘aligned’ (often traditionally, ‘righteous’)

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Beating one’s chest was a cultural display of mourning.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: Literally, “Look!” The word idou is used in a variety of ways, including to draw attention, introduce something surprising, or mark a turning point.

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: Most likely referring to the Sanhedrin, the leading body in Jerusalem.

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘good.’ That rendering is not wrong, but it’s vague and too often has come to be understood to mean ‘rule following’ or ‘earning the approval of an authority/God.’ This word is also used in many ways, but they have at their core a sense of being beneficial to others.

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: This word is dikaios, traditionally ‘righteous.’ The word is related to ‘just’ or ‘straight’ or ‘aligned’ and it usually refers to being aligned with Torah and justice, the path of the Lord. In this case, it is referring directly to alignment with God or the path traced out by Torah and lived out by Jesus.

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: Cut into the stone like a cave

footnotes.label: nn
footnotes.html: The day of preparation is the day before Shabbat, when all the preparations would be made so that no work would have to be done on Shabbat, so the day ‘after the day of preparation’ would be Shabbat.

footnotes.label: oo
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘dawning’ from a word that means ‘to grow light’ but Sabbath starts at sundown Friday, and the image of dawn was figurative for the beginning of the day despite being in the evening.

footnotes.label: pp
footnotes.html: Or ‘remained quiet’ or ‘held their peace’ or ‘lived quietly,’ or ‘remained still’ or ‘remained undisturbed.’ Not only did they follow the direction to rest on Shabbat, they exercised patience in waiting to visit the tomb. Unhurried, non-anxious presence is the focus of Shabbat rest and peace. Walter Brueggemann’s Sabbath as Resistance is a good resource for a fuller picture of what is involved in the values behind Shabbat observance.

footnotes.label: qq
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘commandment’
